title: 30 Years of RFCs
summary: Marks the 30th anniversary of the RFC series with a recollection from the then RFC Editor Joyce K. Reynolds, followed by recollections from pioneers Steve Crocker, who wrote RFC 1, Vint Cerf and Jake Feinler. It is informational and was later updated by RFC 8700.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo marks thirty years of the RFC series with recollections from people who wrote, edited, and distributed early RFCs. It describes the series' origins, its working style, and its growth through 1999.

questions: when was the first rfc published
subtitle: Recollections from people involved in the RFC series, marking its thirtieth anniversary in 1999.

tldr.problem: In 1999, the RFC series reached thirty years, and its contributors wanted to record how it began and how it developed.
tldr.mechanism: The commemorative memo collects recollections from Robert Braden, Joyce K. Reynolds, Steve Crocker, Vint Cerf, Jake Feinler, and Celeste Anderson, alongside an appendix reproducing RFC 1's title information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2555 is an Informational commemorative memo, not a technical specification. The unit metadata lists RFC 8700 as updating it.

today: RFC 2555 is an Informational commemorative memo published in April 1999 and was updated by RFC 8700. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: A Thirtieth-Anniversary Collection
sections.content:
RFC 2555 marks thirty years since RFC 1 appeared at UCLA. Its introduction says the series contained more than 2500 networking documents and that Jon Postel had collected, archived, and edited it for 28 years. The memo is offered as a tribute after Postel's death.

The collection includes recollections by the then RFC Editor Joyce K. Reynolds, Steve Crocker, who wrote RFC 1, Vint Cerf, Jake Feinler, and Celeste Anderson.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC series reached its thirtieth anniversary in 1999. People who helped create and maintain it contributed recollections for this commemorative memo.

sections.title: Reynolds on RFC Editing
sections.content:
Joyce K. Reynolds recalls working with Jon Postel on IP network number and protocol parameter assignments. She noticed documents awaiting publication accumulating in folders on his desk. When she suggested sharing the workload, Postel moved a computer stand stacked with documents into her office and said, “I'm letting go!”

The stack included the NLS Textbook. Reynolds explains that the NLS system was used by Postel to write, edit, and create RFCs. She also describes his commitment to consistent style and document quality.
sections.plainLanguage: Reynolds describes how Postel shared a growing publication workload with her. The documents led her to learn about the tools used to write and edit RFCs.

sections.title: Crocker on RFC 1 and the Early Network
sections.content:
Steve Crocker describes RFC 1, “Host Software,” published April 7, 1969, as a modest memo that mattered because it belonged to a wider effort. At the time, the ARPANET was still being designed. The first four planned nodes were UCLA, SRI, the University of California, Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah.

Crocker recalls that early discussions considered applications before detailed network specifications were available. Ideas included downloadable programs to control sessions and make efficient use of limited bandwidth. He identifies an open, layered architecture and an informal process for discussing design as important early choices. The RFC numbering and distribution system was intended to start a dialogue, not assert control.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 1 recorded early ideas while the ARPANET was still being designed. Crocker says the informal, open process helped participants discuss and develop the network's design.

sections.title: Cerf on How the RFC Series Changed
sections.content:
Vint Cerf describes the transition from tentative RFC discussions to more structured documents as the Internet became more important. He credits Steve Crocker, Jon Postel, Joyce K. Reynolds, and Bob Braden, and recalls how RFCs included technical documents, poetry, humor, and reference material.

Cerf describes how Internet-related note series were merged into the RFC series after Internet protocols were mandated on the ARPANET and other DARPA-sponsored networks. He also describes the growth of the IETF, the development of standards-track RFCs, and the use of Internet-Drafts as working documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC series became more formal as the Internet grew, but it retained material beyond technical standards. The process and organizations responsible for producing RFCs also changed over time.

sections.title: Feinler and Anderson on Distribution and Memory
sections.content:
Jake Feinler recalls that RFC 2 appeared two days after RFC 1 and that RFC 3 described conventions for the notes. RFC 3 allowed notes from anyone, encouraged timely rather than polished writing, and set a minimum length of one sentence. Feinler describes the SRI NLS Journal, which let readers retrieve full documents through links, and the Network Information Center's role in distributing documents.

Feinler says RFCs were shared freely and were never restricted or classified. She recalls that when she left the NIC project in 1989, there were about 30,000 Internet hosts and just over 1000 RFCs. Celeste Anderson describes plans for a collection of favorite RFCs for the anniversary; the memo invited readers to vote, with voting closing December 31, 1999. Its Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The recollections describe how early RFCs were written, found, and distributed, and how the series grew. The final contribution invited readers to choose RFCs for an anniversary collection.
